passage:
Every Thursday after five-a-side in Manchester, Bilal and Marek sat in the car park eating chips. Lately Marek did most of the talking.
'I went to Mass on Sunday for the first time in a year,' Marek said. 'Sat at the back. Felt like a visitor. Then I read half of a book arguing there's no God and felt like a visitor there too.'
Bilal had his own answers. He prayed five times a day, and it steadied him. He could have said so. He could have offered a clever argument.
Instead he asked, 'Which part felt most like home?'
Marek thought about it. 'The singing, maybe. Not the words. The people.'
'Then maybe start there,' Bilal said, and passed him the vinegar.
They sat until the floodlights went off.

qa.q: What did Marek read half of?
qa.a: He read half of a book arguing there's no God.

qa.q: How does Bilal feel as he holds back his own answers?
qa.a: Bilal feels steady and secure in his own faith, but he cares more about Marek than about winning, so he asks a question instead of offering a clever argument.

qa.q: Why is Bilal's question better than a clever argument?
qa.a: Asking which part felt like home keeps the focus on Marek's own experience, so Marek feels accompanied rather than argued with.

qa.q: How might Marek experience these Thursday talks with Bilal?
qa.a: Marek likely feels safe to think aloud, since Bilal listens instead of trying to win him over.

grounding: It shows a friend of another faith listening to a seeker's doubts without trying to convert him or score points.

At 3 am the nurses' break room at the city hospital was quiet except for the humming fridge. Dilnaz stirred her tea for far too long.
'My navjote was the proudest day of my parents' lives,' she said. 'Now I read about Zarathustra and the fire temple and I don't know if I believe any of it. Or if I just love my grandmother.'
Zeenat's prayer mat was folded in her locker; she had prayed Fajr at the end of night shifts for years. She could have said, try what works for me. She didn't.
'What are you reading?' she asked instead.
Dilnaz showed her. They talked it through, Zeenat asking questions, not giving answers, until a monitor alarm down the ward called them back.
'Thanks for not trying to fix me,' Dilnaz said, rinsing her cup.
'You're not broken,' Zeenat said. 'You're thinking.'

qa.q: What does Zeenat keep folded in her locker?
qa.a: Zeenat keeps her prayer mat folded in her locker.

qa.q: What doubt is Dilnaz feeling when she mentions her grandmother?
qa.a: Dilnaz is unsure whether she truly believes or whether her attachment is mostly love for her grandmother.

qa.q: What does Zeenat do that makes Dilnaz feel accompanied?
qa.a: She asks about the reading and poses questions without offering her own path as the answer, so Dilnaz can think aloud safely.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz experience Zeenat's listening?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels grateful and understood, thanking Zeenat for not trying to fix her.

grounding: It shows a colleague of another faith accompanying a seeker's doubts with questions rather than persuasion.

passage:
Dear Tanvir,
Last night on the terrace, when you said you weren't sure any more what you believed, I could see how much it cost you to say it. I just want you to know I'm glad you told me.
I'm not going to try to bring you round to my side, or anyone's. You know I go to the temple with my grandmother and that I'm not very sure about half of it myself. What I believe isn't the point. I'm not keeping score.
If you want to talk about what you're reading, I'm here. If you go to Friday prayers some weeks and not others, I'll still save you a samosa afterwards. If you just want to sit on the terrace and not talk, that's fine too.
You don't need a debate partner. You need a friend who stays. That's all I'm offering.
Gautam

qa.q: Where were Gautam and Tanvir last night?
qa.a: On the terrace.

qa.q: What did Gautam feel seeing how much it cost Tanvir to speak?
qa.a: Gautam felt moved and protective, glad to be trusted with something so hard.

qa.q: Why is Gautam's offer the right kind of support?
qa.a: Gautam refuses to convert or argue and simply offers to listen and stay, which a person in doubt needs most.

qa.q: What might Tanvir feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Tanvir likely feels relieved and less alone, accompanied rather than argued with.

grounding: A friend of another faith writes to a seeker offering company and listening, with no attempt to convert or win points.

passage:
People ask me how I helped Ankita through her year of doubt. Honestly, I didn't do much, and I think that's why it helped.
She grew up in a devout Christian family in Shillong. When the questions started, everyone around her had an agenda. Her church friends wanted to pull her back. A cousin who didn't believe sent her videos to pull her out. She told me she felt like the rope in a tug-of-war.
I'm not Christian, and I'm not an atheist either; I light a lamp for my grandmother and leave it at that. So I just listened. Every Sunday we walked around Ward's Lake, and she talked: about hell, about her father, about a psalm she still loved. I asked questions. I never said what she should conclude.
Once she said, "You're the only one who doesn't want something from me." That's when I understood. I'm Bhupen, and my only job was to walk beside her.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen and Ankita walk on Sundays?
qa.a: Around Ward's Lake.

qa.q: What did Bhupen feel on hearing Ankita say nobody else wanted nothing from her?
qa.a: Bhupen felt a quiet understanding and warmth, realising that simply accompanying Ankita was what was needed.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that the others didn't?
qa.a: Bhupen listened and asked questions without pushing a conclusion, instead of pulling Ankita toward any side.

qa.q: What was Ankita's year of doubt like, pulled by everyone?
qa.a: Ankita felt torn and pressured, like the rope in a tug-of-war, with everyone wanting something from her.

grounding: A friend of a different belief accompanies a seeker on weekly walks, listening without trying to convert or score points.

passage:
I've known Vikas since college, and this year I've watched him wrestle with his faith the way other people wrestle with a job offer.
He comes over on Thursday nights with a pile of books: the Gita, a book on Buddhism, essays by a scientist. He reads passages aloud and argues with them. Some nights he's excited. Some nights he just stares at the wall. I can't tell exactly what he feels; he doesn't always say.
I'm a practising Sikh, and I go to the gurdwara most Sundays. It would be easy to say, "Come with me, it'll help." I haven't. When he asked what I believe, I told him honestly and briefly, then asked what he thought.
Last week he said, "You're the only person who hasn't tried to recruit me." I laughed and made him another cup of tea. I'm Payal. My job isn't to win him over. It's to keep the kettle on.

qa.q: What does Vikas bring on Thursday nights?
qa.a: A pile of books.

qa.q: What does Payal feel when tempted to say 'Come with me'?
qa.a: Payal feels caring and tempted to help in a familiar way, but holds back out of respect for Vikas's search.

qa.q: Why is Payal's approach what Vikas needs?
qa.a: Answering honestly when asked but never recruiting lets Vikas feel accompanied rather than argued with.

qa.q: What is this year like for Vikas?
qa.a: Vikas swings between excitement and blankness, wrestling seriously with big questions, and values a friend who doesn't push.

grounding: A friend of another faith keeps a seeker company through a year of doubt, answering honestly but never recruiting or arguing.

passage:
Tuesday: Irfan called Aditi late from the hospital canteen where they both worked night shifts. "I skipped Friday prayers again. I don't know what I believe anymore." Aditi, who went to the Ganesh temple every week, wanted to say something wise. She just said, "Tell me more."
Two weeks later: they walked by the lake, and Irfan listed the questions that kept him up. Aditi could have told him what her own tradition said about suffering. She didn't. She asked which question hurt the most.
A month after that: Irfan said he had started reading with an imam who welcomed questions, and also a book by an atheist writer. "You never once tried to win," he told her. Aditi shrugged, but she felt a small glow of pride. She had been scared, at the start, of saying the wrong thing. Now she knew listening was enough.

qa.q: Where did Irfan call Aditi from on Tuesday?
qa.a: He called her from the hospital canteen where they both worked night shifts.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel at the start, and how did that change?
qa.a: Aditi was scared at first of saying the wrong thing, and by the end she felt a small glow of pride, knowing that listening was enough.

qa.q: How did Aditi support Irfan as a friend of a different belief?
qa.a: She kept asking questions and listening, never pushing her own tradition's answers, so Irfan could search without feeling argued with.

qa.q: What is it like for Irfan to be accompanied this way?
qa.a: Irfan feels safe and not judged, free to read with an imam and an atheist writer, and grateful that his friend never tried to win.

grounding: Shows a friend of a different belief listening to a seeker without trying to convert them or win the argument, and the seeker feeling accompanied.
